title: Measuring Verifier Impact in an LLM Generate→Verify→Repair Loop for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We measure how inserting a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) loop affects verifier-detected safety violations for LLM-produced device-configuration proposals. In a preregistered paired design (N = 500 intent→configuration tasks stratified across VLAN-change, ACL-change, and static-route-change clusters) we compared: (1) baseline — a single LLM proposal produced once per task, and (2) guarded — the identical shared LLM proposal validated by a deterministic netops verifier and subjected to up to one automated repair iteration if the verifier flagged a preregistered high/medium-severity violation. Primary outcome: verifier pass (no preregistered high/medium-severity violations). Results (complete pairs = 500): baseline passed 499/500 (0.998), guarded passed 500/500 (1.000); contingency: n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002; paired-bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). The preregistered exact McNemar two-sided test was implemented as an exact binomial on discordant pairs (n = n10 + n01); with n = 1 and n10 = 1 the archived two-sided p = 1.00 under that convention. Interpretation: on this verifier-scoped synthetic corpus and model+validator pairing the LLM produced near-ceiling proposals; measured marginal verifier+repair effect on the pass-rate metric is therefore small, though the verifier corrected at least one concrete baseline failure. All preregistration, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle for deterministic re-inspection.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are being applied to NetOps tasks such as translation of operator intent to device configuration, multi-step change planning, and programmatic repairs. System reports and surveys emphasize that operational safety depends heavily on surrounding engineering: deterministic validators, sandbox replay, canarying, and rollback mechanisms [Beckett et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. A widely proposed operational pattern is generate→verify→repair (G→V→R): an LLM generates a candidate configuration, a deterministic verifier checks a set of formalized properties, and automated or human-in-the-loop repairs are applied for violations.

Despite conceptual consensus, controlled measurements that isolate the marginal contribution of a verifier (holding the model’s proposal fixed) are scarce in the published record. Practitioners must know: when an LLM already produces high-quality candidates, how much incremental safety does a verifier plus a modest automated repair budget provide on a verifier-scoped pass/fail metric? To answer this precisely we preregistered and executed a paired experiment that isolates verifier+repair impact under canonical, deterministic semantics. Our objective was deliberately narrow and operational: given identical initial proposals (shared-initial_candidate semantics), how much does integrating a deterministic verifier and at most one automated repair iteration reduce verifier-detected safety violations compared to the same LLM alone?
sections.related_work:
Formal and deterministic verification tools for network configurations and update-safety (header-space analysis, route-model verifiers, Batfish-style analyzers) provide machine-checkable properties such as reachability/isolation and update atomicity; these methods are established in NetOps verification literature and motivate verifier-in-the-loop system designs [Beckett et al., 2017]. Concurrently, recent NetOps/AIOps systems and intent-translation research demonstrate integrations of LLMs for intent parsing and configuration generation while advocating guardrails for operational reliability (e.g., INTA, Confucius, other agentic NetOps frameworks) [INTA, 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. Generate–verify–repair patterns appear across structured generation domains and have been proposed to reduce incorrect or unsafe outputs [PoeTone; INTA].

Separate literature documents systemic failure modes of LLM-driven automation (hallucination, overconfidence, tool-integration errors) and recommends verification or human oversight as mitigations [Owen, 2026; DeepSeek-AI, 2025]. What is less prevalent in the supplied evidence is a controlled, preregistered ablation that quantifies the marginal verifier effect while keeping the LLM’s initial output identical for both arms. Our study contributes such an artifact-backed measurement and places it in the context of those prior system reports and verification methods.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory plan. We preregistered study_id cand_7f4b9a2d_hosted_gvr_v1_2026, freezing research questions, inclusion/exclusion rules, task generator seeds, estimands, analysis executor, multiplicity plan, retry policy, and stopping rule before observing outcomes. Primary confirmatory hypothesis: an LLM paired with a deterministic verifier plus a single automated repair iteration will produce a lower verifier-detected safety-violation rate than the same LLM producing a single proposal without verifier feedback (paired within-task). Primary estimand: the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline where success == verifier reports zero preregistered high/medium-severity violations. The preregistration and all supporting artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle (preregistration SHA-256 recorded in the execution manifest).

Task generation and strata. A deterministic synthetic corpus of 500 intent→configuration tasks was created using deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 with preregistered seeds. Tasks were stratified into three clusters: VLAN-change (167), ACL-change (167), static-route-change (166). The generator constrained allowed_features to {admin, mtu, vlan} to match the deterministic verifier’s modeled scope; the full task manifest (inputs, seeds, expected_final_state, required_sequence) is archived under execution/task_manifest.jsonl. The preregistration specified deterministic replacement rules for excluded or duplicate tasks; no confirmatory exclusions occurred in this run.

Generation semantics and experiment control. To isolate the verifier’s marginal effect we used generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" (independent_condition_generation = false). For each task the pipeline produced a single shared LLM proposal (shared candidate) recorded once; that identical candidate constituted the baseline output and was also validated by the guarded arm. The guarded path invoked the automated single-repair call only if the deterministic verifier reported a preregistered high/medium-severity violation on the shared candidate. This semantics prevents conflation with verifier-guided regeneration and isolates the effect of verification plus at most one repair applied to the same initial proposal.

Models, adapter, and verifier. Requested LLM = gpt-5-mini called through the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter (provider recorded as openai_responses); execution/model_configuration.json in the archive records model parameters (max_output_tokens = 2000, single-attempt generation). The deterministic verifier used for gating and scoring was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator specification and the mapping of violation codes to severity are archived). The guarded arm permitted at most one automated repair iteration per preregistered contract.

Primary statistical test and exact implementation. The preregistered confirmatory test was an exact McNemar two-sided test on paired binary outcomes. The archived analysis executor implements the exact two-sided McNemar by forming n = n10 + n01 (discordant pairs) and performing an exact binomial test B(n, 0.5) on the observed count n10 (the number of pairs where guarded passes and baseline fails, per the executor’s discordant ordering convention). The two-sided p-value is computed as p_two-sided = 2 × min{P(X ≤ n10), P(X ≥ n10)} for X ∼ Binomial(n, 0.5), truncated at 1.0. For the observed discordant counts (n10 = 1, n01 = 0) this produces p = 1.00; the archived implementation and rationale are recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl. We report that archived exact two-sided p = 1.00 and contextualize it in Results.

Bootstrap CI and resampling. Paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CIs were computed for the absolute difference using B = 10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729. Resampling unit = task/pair with pairing preserved (each bootstrap draw samples 500 pairs with replacement). The bootstrap parameters and code references are archived in analysis artifacts.

Missingness, retries, and stopping rule. The preregistered retry policy allowed up to two automated retries for transient model-provider errors. The run stopped after successful processing of the preregistered confirmatory pairs or when the adapter model-call budget was reached. Execution accounting (execution manifest) recorded model_calls_used = 501 and completed_episode_count = 1000 (500 pairs × shared generation plus one repair-stage call observed); failed_episode_count = 0. All provider call traces, responses, and retry metadata are archived.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary outcomes. The run completed with complete_pair_count = 500 and model_calls_used = 501 (shared_initial_generation = 500; repair-stage calls = 1). Aggregated per-condition counts (analysis/condition_summary.csv): baseline successes = 499, baseline failures = 1 (baseline_success_rate = 0.998); guarded successes = 500, guarded failures = 0 (guarded_success_rate = 1.000). The paired contingency table (guarded × baseline; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is: n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002.

Exact McNemar two-sided p-value and CI. Using the archived exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention described above yields two-sided p = 1.00 for the observed discordant counts (n = 1, n10 = 1). The paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute difference is [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). The analysis artifacts (analysis/results.json and the CSVs) and the analysis_log.jsonl record these computations and parameters.

Repair activity and provenance of the discordant pair. Observed repair-stage provider calls = 1. That single repair produced the sole discordant outcome (n10 = 1): the guarded arm converted one baseline-detected violation into a verified pass. The evidence bundle archives per-task validator diagnostics, normalized configurations, repair prompts/responses (when invoked), and provider-call traces. Because the exact pair identifier for the discordant episode is recorded in execution/raw_results.jsonl rather than listed in the manuscript text, readers can deterministically locate it by filtering that file for entries where baseline scoring indicates a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass == 0) and guarded scoring indicates a pass (guarded pass == 1). The manifest and deterministic_reconciliation.json confirm exactly one such episode exists; the run-level fields model_calls_used = 501 and repair-stage calls = 1 match the per-task archival traces. Representative per-task exemplar files and provider-call traces are included in the evidence bundle (see artifact_examples and representative_tasks entries).

Secondary analyses and power divergence. The preregistration planned power assuming a baseline error prevalence p_b ≈ 0.30 (N ≈ 384 for 80% power to detect a 10-percentage-point absolute reduction). Observed baseline failure prevalence was far lower (1/500), producing a ceiling effect that reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute improvements. As a consequence the preregistered power assumption did not hold and secondary per-violation-class analyses were uninformative due to near-zero counts. All relevant diagnostics (missingness_summary.csv, contamination_summary.csv, and deterministic_reconciliation.json) indicate no exclusions, no contamination flags, and zero failed episodes under the execution contract.

Representative examples. The evidence bundle contains multiple representative task records (execution/responses and execution/scoring JSON artifacts). Example: task-000001 (example archived under representative_tasks) shows a medium-difficulty shutdown→configure→restore pattern where both baseline and guarded produced an identical valid configuration and the verifier reported zero violations; task payloads and expected_final_state are archived for deterministic inspection. The single corrected episode's full validator diagnostics and repair-stage prompt/response are available in execution/raw_results.jsonl and associated provider-call traces; since we must not invent identifiers, we provide the retrieval method above so readers and auditors can locate the episode deterministically.
sections.discussion:
Operational interpretation. Under the constrained experimental regime — single requested LLM (gpt-5-mini), deterministic shared-initial_candidate semantics, a deterministic verifier modeling a limited feature set (allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}), and at most one automated repair iteration — the LLM produced near-ceiling correct proposals and the marginal measured pass-rate benefit of adding the verifier was small (0.002). This is a conditional result: it documents that when baseline proposal quality (on verifier-scoped properties) is very high, measurable pass-rate gains from modest verifier+repair budgets may be negligible on a composite pass/fail metric. Importantly, the verifier still exhibited corrective utility by converting one concrete baseline failure into a pass (the single discordant episode archived in raw_results.jsonl).

Design-choice implications. The shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally isolate the verifier+repair effect conditional on identical proposals. This answers the specific operational question of marginal verifier benefit when regeneration costs are constrained or when deployment semantics require a single human-reviewed proposal to be repaired rather than regenerated. The design does not evaluate alternative operational choices such as verifier-guided regeneration, multiple repair iterations, or cost-weighted objective functions; those alternatives may produce different effect sizes and should be measured under their own preregistrations.

Threats to validity. Internal validity is supported by preregistration, deterministic task seeds, and automated replacement rules; no manual adjudication occurred. Construct validity is limited by the verifier’s modeled property set: pass==no high/medium-severity violations is defined relative to the verifier’s coverage and severity mapping archived in the validator-spec artifacts. If production operators care about properties outside that modeled set (vendor-specific CLI behaviors, dynamic protocol states), the measured pass-rate difference here underestimates the operational benefit of broader verifier coverage. External validity is limited by single-model testing, synthetic task corpus, and constrained feature scope; results are not evidence of multi-model or cross-vendor generality.

Statistical nuance and interpretation. The archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 reflects the executor’s exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs computation and the empirical discordant counts (n = 1). Small-sample exact p-values under such conventions can be non-intuitive; here p = 1.00 indicates the observed discordant pattern (one guarded-only success, zero baseline-only successes) is not unusual under the null when n is so small. The paired-bootstrap CI [0.0, 0.006] provides a complementary uncertainty quantification for the absolute difference. Together these artifacts show that while a point-estimate improvement exists (0.002), inference is constrained by a ceiling effect and by the small number of discordant outcomes.

Operational recommendations. (1) Measure baseline proposal error prevalence on representative operational data before allocating expensive repair budgets: when baseline error is extremely low on verifier-scoped properties, marginal pass-rate gains per unit cost may be small. (2) Align verifier property coverage with operator-critical constraints; inspect the archived validator-spec to determine modeled properties and severity mapping and expand verifier coverage where needed. (3) Choose generation semantics to match operational priorities: shared-initial semantics minimize model-call overhead and preserve the original proposal for human review, whereas verifier-guided regeneration may increase final-pass probability at the cost of additional model calls.

Reproducibility and auditability. All artifacts required to reproduce the run are archived in the evidence bundle: preregistration, task generator code and seeds, model_configuration.json, execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, provider-call traces, validator traces, analysis CSVs, and the deterministic_reconciliation manifest. The execution manifest records model_calls_used = 501 and observed repair-stage calls = 1. The exact initial master prompt starting the autonomous research run is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA-256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba) and is referenced in the Disclosure Statement. The single discordant episode is locatable deterministically by filtering execution/raw_results.jsonl for baseline pass==0 and guarded pass==1; the run-level artifacts confirm there is exactly one such episode.
sections.conclusion: We performed a preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment (N = 500) that isolated the verifier+single-repair effect under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The LLM produced near-ceiling verifier-scoped proposals (baseline 499/500; guarded 500/500), giving an absolute improvement of 0.002 (95% CI [0.0, 0.006]; archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 under the run’s exact-binomial convention). This conditional measurement illustrates a ceiling-effect regime: when baseline proposal quality is very high for the verifier-modeled properties and the verifier’s coverage is limited, the measurable marginal pass-rate benefit of a modest verifier+repair budget can be negligible on a composite pass/fail metric, though the verifier can still correct rare concrete failures. We recommend practitioners measure baseline error prevalence on representative workloads, align verifier coverage with operator-critical properties, and select generation/repair semantics that match deployment priorities. The full preregistration, code, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle for deterministic re-inspection of every claim made here.

Preregistration and execution artifacts: the preregistration preceded execution and was archived (preregistration SHA-256 recorded in the execution manifest); execution artifacts include model_configuration.json and execution manifests. Generation semantics and model-call accounting (artifact-backed): preregistered generation_semantics = 'shared_initial_candidate' with independent_condition_generation = false: for each task the pipeline produced a single shared initial LLM proposal that served as the baseline and was also validated by the guarded arm; the guarded arm invoked a repair-stage provider call only when the validator reported preregistered high/medium-severity violations on that shared candidate. Repairs: the guarded arm permitted up to one automated repair iteration per preregistration; observed repairs = 1. limitations: Synthetic, deterministic task corpus limited to features modeled by the deterministic validator; task payloads constrained to allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}. Results do not generalize to unconstrained production intents, cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity, or protocol semantics outside the verifier scope.
Single requested model family (gpt-5-mini requested) and a single validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) — no claim of multi-model or cross-validator generality is made.
Maximum one automated repair iteration was permitted by the preregistration; different repair budgets or iterative regeneration strategies could change measured verifier impact.

Very high baseline pass rate (499/500) created a ceiling effect that limits power to detect small absolute improvements on the pass-rate metric; the archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 reflects the archived exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention and the small discordant count.

The single discordant episode (the sole task where baseline failed and guarded succeeded) and its validator diagnostics and repair-stage trace are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl in the evidence bundle. To inspect it deterministically: filter execution/raw_results.jsonl for pair entries where the baseline scoring outcome indicates a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass == 0) while the guarded scoring outcome indicates pass == 1; because only one such discordant pair exists in the confirmatory set, this lookup returns the single episode and its provider-call traces. The validator violation-code→severity mapping is archived in the execution manifest and validator-spec artifacts in the bundle.
